extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate (or beginning graduate) students and instructors in real analysis/advanced calculus
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter on continuity covering the intermediate value theorem (Bolzano), extreme/intermediate value consequences, the bisection method, uniform continuity, Lipschitz continuity, and limits at infinity, with proofs, examples, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (bisection lemma) for root existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b]→ℝ be continuous and suppose f(a)<0 and f(b)>0. Then there exists c in (a,b) such that f(c)=0. The proof constructs nested intervals [a_n,b_n] recursively (bisecting at midpoints and choosing the subinterval where the sign change persists), producing monotone bounded sequences whose limits agree; continuity then gives f(c)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via bisection yields a convergent sequence of interval endpoints; this is the basis of the bisection method in numerical root finding. The lemma is used as the building block for the intermediate value theorem; see Figure 3.7 and Example 3.3.9 for an applied bisection demonstration and precision control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bolzano’s intermediate value theorem (IVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b]→ℝ be continuous. If y is between f(a) and f(b) (i.e. f(a)<y<f(b) or f(b)<y<f(a)), then there exists c in [a,b] such that f(c)=y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to the lemma above. The theorem guarantees that a continuous function on a closed interval attains every value between its endpoint values; practical consequence: whenever you find an interval where the endpoints' function values straddle a target y, a root/value exists. Note: continuity on a closed interval is essential (see examples showing failure otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bisection method (algorithmic application of IVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the lemma/proof of IVT one can iteratively bisect an interval where a sign change occurs to approximate a root to any desired precision in finitely many steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method applies to any continuous function (not just polynomials). Advantage: simplicity and guaranteed convergence when IVT conditions hold. Example 3.3.9 walks through approximating a polynomial root and discusses precision and termination criteria; other methods (Newton) may be faster but less globally robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: image of continuous function on [a,b] is closed and bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:[a,b]→ℝ is continuous, then the direct image f([a,b]) is a closed and bounded interval or a single number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from combining the extreme/intermediate value results in the section. It implies completeness properties of images of continuous maps on compact intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odd-degree polynomial has a real root
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is a polynomial of odd degree d (with leading coefficient nonzero), then f has a real root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaling to monic and comparing the highest-order term vs. lower-order terms shows that for large positive n the polynomial is positive and for large negative n it is negative (when degree is odd), so IVT yields a root. See Proposition 3.3.10 and Exercise 3.3.5 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of k-th root of positive number via IVT
rubrics_metrics.description: For any integer k≥1 and any y>0 there exists x>0 such that x^k = y. Proof: consider f(x)=x^k - y and apply Bolzano's theorem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case yields existence of square root √2 etc.; this is a simple application of IVT to monotone continuous functions on [0,∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate value property does not imply continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist discontinuous functions that have the intermediate value property (IVP); e.g., f(x)=sin(1/x) for x≠0 and f(0)=0 has the IVP but is not continuous at 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 3.3.4 asks to show this; it highlights that IVP is strictly weaker than continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of uniform continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f:S⊂ℝ→ℝ is uniformly continuous if for every ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that whenever x,c∈S and |x-c|<δ then |f(x)-f(c)|<ε. The δ depends only on ε and not on the point c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform continuity implies ordinary continuity. Domain matters: a function may be continuous but not uniformly continuous on a larger set yet become uniformly continuous when restricted to a closed bounded interval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem: continuous on closed bounded interval ⇒ uniformly continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f:[a,b]→ℝ be continuous. Then f is uniformly continuous on [a,b].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contrapositive uses sequences violating uniform continuity and Bolzano–Weierstrass to extract a convergent subsequence whose limit lies in [a,b]; then continuity at that limit yields a contradiction. Key hypotheses: closedness and boundedness of the domain (compactness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: uniformly continuous functions preserve Cauchy sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If f:S⊂ℝ→ℝ is uniformly continuous and (x_n) is a Cauchy sequence in S, then (f(x_n)) is a Cauchy sequence in ℝ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given ε>0 pick δ for uniform continuity and use Cauchy property to find N with |x_n-x_k|<δ for n,k≥N, then |f(x_n)-f(x_k)|<ε. This lemma underlies continuous extension results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: uniform continuity ⇔ continuous extendability to endpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f:(a,b)→ℝ is uniformly continuous iff the one-sided limits L_a = lim_{x→a+} f(x) and L_b = lim_{x→b-} f(x) exist; in that case f extends to a continuous function on [a,b] by defining those endpoint values accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction uses Theorem 3.4.4 (restriction of continuous extension is uniformly continuous). The other direction uses Lemma 3.4.5: uniform continuity sends Cauchy sequences to Cauchy sequences, so sequences approaching an endpoint produce a Cauchy image sequence with a limit independent of chosen sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Lipschitz continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: f:S⊂ℝ→ℝ is Lipschitz continuous if there exists K such that |f(x)-f(y)| ≤ K|x-y| for all x,y in S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric interpretation: every secant line slope between two graph points has absolute value ≤K. Lipschitz continuity implies uniform continuity; choice δ=ε/K proves implication. Domains matter: some functions are Lipschitz on restricted intervals but not globally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: Lipschitz ⇒ uniformly continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Lipschitz with constant K on S then for any ε>0 choosing δ=ε/K yields |x-y|<δ ⇒ |f(x)-f(y)|<ε, so f is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a simple sufficient condition for uniform continuity and a quantitative modulus of continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating domain dependence of Lipschitz/ uniform continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sine and cosine are Lipschitz (K=1) on ℝ. The function √x is Lipschitz on [1,∞) (and uniformly continuous on [0,1]) but √x is not Lipschitz on (0,∞). A function can be uniformly continuous on a closed interval but not Lipschitz on an open or unbounded domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to test hypotheses: check domain and behavior near singularities (e.g., slope blow-up near 0) when assessing Lipschitz property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions: limits at infinity and cluster points
rubrics_metrics.description: For f:S⊂ℝ→ℝ and a cluster point at infinity: lim_{x→∞} f(x)=L means for every ε>0 there exists M such that whenever x∈S and x≥M then |f(x)-L|<ε. Similar definitions for x→−∞. A cluster point of S at ∞ means sufficiently large elements of S exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits at infinity are unique if they exist. Distinguish continuous-variable limits from sequence limits (use explicit domain specification when ambiguous).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential characterization of limits at infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lemma 3.5.5: For f:S⊂ℝ→ℝ and L∈ℝ, lim_{x→∞} f(x)=L iff for every sequence (x_n) in S with x_n→∞ we have f(x_n)→L.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parallels the finite-point sequential criterion and is useful for proving or disproving limits via subsequences; e.g., showing nonexistence by producing two sequences tending to ∞ whose images have different limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of infinite limit (divergence to ∞)
rubrics_metrics.description: f(x)→∞ as x→∞ means: for every N∈ℝ there exists M such that whenever x∈S and x≥M, f(x)>N. (Similarly for −∞.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes divergent behavior; can be treated via sequences similarly to finite limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rule for limits (including limits at ∞)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition 3.5.8: Suppose f:A→B and g:B→ℝ with a cluster point a of A and b=lim_{x→a} f(x). If b is a cluster point of B and lim_{y→b} g(y)=c (including the cases b or c being ±∞ allowed) then lim_{x→a} g(f(x))=c. If b∈B and g is continuous at b, the composition limit equals g(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard limit-composition rule; continuity of g at the intermediate limit simplifies hypotheses. Exercise-level proofs and applications are indicated.
